summary: Describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax, a format for digitally signing, digesting, authenticating or encrypting arbitrary message content. It is a building block used by S/MIME and many other security systems. It was replaced by RFC 5652.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is a message format for carrying content with digital signatures, digests, authentication codes, or encryption. RFC 3852 defines six content types and was later replaced by RFC 5652.

questions: what is enveloped data in cms
what are the six cms content types
subtitle: A syntax for signing, digesting, authenticating, and encrypting message content.

tldr.problem: Protocols need a common way to carry arbitrary content together with signatures, encrypted keys, digests, or authentication codes. They may also need to layer more than one protection around the same content.
tldr.mechanism: CMS wraps content in ContentInfo and defines data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data, and authenticated-data content types. These types can be nested.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3852 obsoletes RFC 3369 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 5652. It was also updated by RFC 4853 and RFC 5083.

facts.label: Required recipient key methods
facts.value: Key transport, key agreement, and symmetric key-encryption keys

today: RFC 3852 was obsoleted by RFC 5652 and updated by RFC 4853 and RFC 5083. RFC 3852 itself obsoletes RFC 3369.

sections.title: What CMS Is and Where It Came From
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is an encapsulation format for signing, digesting, authenticating, or encrypting arbitrary content. CMS values are described with ASN.1 and encoded using BER. One CMS object can be placed inside another, and attributes such as signing time can be included.

CMS derives from PKCS #7 version 1.5. The RFC says the IETF had taken responsibility for its development and that several IETF standards-track protocols used it. CMS does not specify particular cryptographic algorithms; other specifications select algorithms for their use.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS defines a structure for carrying data and cryptographic protection information. Other specifications can choose which algorithms to use with that structure.

sections.title: ContentInfo and Six Content Types
sections.content:
ContentInfo identifies a content type with an object identifier and carries the associated content. RFC 3852 defines six types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data, and authenticated-data. A content type may encapsulate another type, and additional content types can be defined elsewhere.

A conforming implementation must support ContentInfo, data, signed-data, and enveloped-data. The other three types are optional. CMS supports single-pass processing with indefinite-length BER, although signed attributes and authenticated attributes must use DER so recipients can verify them consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: ContentInfo identifies what kind of content is inside a CMS object. The six types provide different combinations of content, signatures, digests, encryption, and authentication.

sections.title: Signed-Data
sections.content:
Signed-data carries content and zero or more digital signatures. Each signer computes a message digest, signs it with a private key, and contributes a SignerInfo value. Certificates and certificate revocation lists may also be included. A recipient independently computes the digest and uses the signer's public key to verify the signature.

When signed attributes are present, they must be DER encoded and include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute. The content itself may be omitted to create an external signature. The recipient must not rely on a digest value supplied by the sender; it computes the value needed for verification.
sections.plainLanguage: Signed-data carries content and a signature that a recipient can check with the signer's public key. The recipient calculates its own digest rather than trusting a digest supplied by the sender.

sections.title: Enveloped-Data and Recipient Keys
sections.content:
Enveloped-data encrypts content with a randomly generated content-encryption key. The sender separately protects that key for each recipient, then includes the encrypted content and recipient information in the CMS value. The same content-encryption algorithm and key protect the content for all recipients.

CMS defines key transport, key agreement, previously distributed symmetric keys, password-based key management, and an extension alternative. Implementations must support key transport, key agreement, and previously distributed symmetric keys. A recipient recovers a key using its recipient-specific information and then decrypts the content.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender encrypts the content once and protects the content key separately for each recipient. A recipient recovers that key and uses it to decrypt the content.

sections.title: Digests, Encryption and Authentication Codes
sections.content:
Digested-data carries content and a message digest that a recipient can recompute. Encrypted-data carries encrypted content without recipient information or encrypted content keys, so keys must be managed separately. The RFC describes local storage as a typical use of encrypted-data.

Authenticated-data carries content, a message authentication code (MAC), and information for recipients to obtain the MAC key. The recipient computes the MAC and compares it with the carried value. If authenticated attributes are present, the format also requires content-type and message-digest attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A digest lets a recipient compare a recalculated value with the transmitted one. Authenticated-data uses a MAC and recipient key information, while encrypted-data leaves key management to another method.

sections.title: Key Protection and Algorithm Strength
sections.content:
The RFC says implementations must protect signing private keys, key-management private keys, key-encryption keys, content-encryption keys, and message-authentication keys. Compromise can permit impersonation, disclosure of encrypted content, or undetectable modification of authenticated content.

Content-encryption keys, MAC keys, initialization vectors, padding, and public/private key pairs depend on suitable randomness. When different algorithms protect a content key and its encrypted copy, the weaker algorithm limits the protection. The RFC recommends modular algorithm implementations so algorithms can change over time.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS security depends on protecting the keys and generating them with adequate randomness. If two algorithms protect the same content, the weaker one limits the overall protection.

viz.caption: The six CMS content types defined in RFC 3852

items.title: enveloped-data
items.text: Carries encrypted content and recipient key information.

items.title: digested-data
items.text: Carries content and its message digest.

items.title: encrypted-data
items.text: Carries encrypted content; keys are managed separately.

items.title: authenticated-data
items.text: Carries content, a MAC, and recipient key information.
